lesson_title: Lesson 11: Reading Multiple-Choice — Inference, Purpose, Context, and Option Analysis

overview.what_it_is: This lesson develops the reading and decision-making skills needed for Reading: Multiple-choice, choose single answer and Reading: Multiple-choice, choose multiple answers. The central challenge is not simply understanding the passage; it is identifying what the prompt asks, locating relevant evidence, recognizing paraphrases, distinguishing explicit information from inference, and rejecting options that are unsupported, exaggerated, incomplete, or contextually inaccurate.

format_facts.label: Item types
format_facts.value: The lesson covers both choose single answer and choose multiple answers.

format_facts.label: Single-answer response
format_facts.value: Only one option should be selected, so the chosen answer must be better supported than every alternative.

format_facts.label: Multiple-answer response
format_facts.value: More than one option may be correct, so each option must be judged independently against the passage.

format_facts.label: Prompt variety
format_facts.value: Prompts may ask about gist, writer’s purpose, organization, inference, explicit information, implicit information, categorization, or the contextual meaning of a word.

format_facts.label: Evidence source
format_facts.value: Correct answers may rest on one sentence, several connected sentences, or the overall meaning and attitude of the passage.

format_facts.label: Time pressure
format_facts.value: The reading section is managed as a whole, so learners must balance accuracy with efficient prompt reading, evidence location, and option elimination.

scoring_factors.name: Answer accuracy
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the selected option or options correctly represent the passage.

scoring_factors.name: Prompt alignment
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the response answers the exact question asked rather than a different question about the same text.

scoring_factors.name: Evidence-based selection
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether each chosen answer can be supported by explicit information, logical inference, writer attitude, or contextual meaning.

scoring_factors.name: Option discipline
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner avoids selecting attractive distractors that contain familiar words but distort the passage.

scoring_factors.name: Multiple-answer control
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether each option is evaluated separately instead of assuming that a certain number of answers must be selected.

critical_rules: Read the prompt carefully before deciding how to approach the passage.
Identify whether the task asks for gist, purpose, detail, inference, organization, categorization, or contextual word meaning.
For a broad inference prompt such as “Which statement can be inferred?”, read the passage before studying the options in detail.
Paraphrase every serious option in simpler words before accepting or rejecting it.
Choose answers supported by the passage, not answers that are generally true in real life.
Treat strong words such as “always,” “only,” “completely,” and “never” with caution unless the passage clearly supports them.
When the prompt says “in the passage,” use the contextual meaning rather than the word’s most familiar dictionary meaning.
In multiple-answer items, test each option independently and do not select an option merely because it partly overlaps with the text.

learning_goals: Identify whether a prompt asks for gist, writer’s purpose, organization, inference, explicit information, implicit information, categorization, or contextual word meaning.
Read efficiently for overall meaning without treating every sentence as equally important.
Distinguish a passage’s main idea from examples, explanations, statistics, and minor supporting details.
Infer conclusions that are strongly supported even when they are not directly stated.
Recognize positive, negative, neutral, approving, doubtful, or critical attitudes through word choice.
Paraphrase answer options accurately before comparing them with the passage.
Use sentence context, surrounding vocabulary, contrast, examples, and word parts to infer unfamiliar meanings.
Eliminate options that are contradicted, unsupported, too broad, too narrow, or based on outside knowledge.
Apply different reading sequences to different prompt types.
Complete single-answer and multiple-answer practice items efficiently under timed conditions.

core_method.name: PROMPT–EVIDENCE–OPTION Method
core_method.summary: Begin by decoding the prompt, then read with a clear purpose. Build a brief understanding of the passage, locate the strongest evidence, translate the answer options into simpler language, eliminate weak choices, and recheck the surviving answer or answers against the exact wording of the prompt.

steps.detail: Underline the key instruction and classify it as gist, purpose, detail, inference, organization, categorization, or vocabulary in context.
For broad gist or inference questions, read the passage first. For a specific word-meaning question, go directly to the target sentence and its surrounding context.
Identify the topic, the writer’s central point, the function of each paragraph, and any important contrast, cause, result, example, or conclusion.
Find the sentence or group of sentences that supports the answer. For inference, combine clues without adding unsupported assumptions.
Restate each option in plain language so that complicated wording does not hide exaggeration, reversal, or missing information.
Reject options that are contradicted, not mentioned, only partly true, too strong, too narrow, or based on a minor detail when the prompt asks for the main idea.
For single answer, choose the best-supported option. For multiple answers, judge every option separately and select only those fully supported.
Read the prompt again, compare the answer with the evidence, and confirm that no important qualifier has been overlooked.

core_method.formula: Prompt type → Reading route → Passage map → Evidence → Option paraphrase → Elimination → Selection → Recheck

techniques.name: Prompt Classification
techniques.purpose: To prevent answering the wrong type of question.
how_to: Circle the main instruction word, such as “mainly,” “purpose,” “inferred,” “according to,” or “in the passage.”
Label the prompt with one category: gist, purpose, detail, inference, organization, categorization, or vocabulary.
Decide whether you need the whole passage or only a focused section.
Keep the prompt category in mind while checking every option.
techniques.example: For “Which statement can be inferred from the passage?”, label the task INFERENCE and search for a conclusion supported by several clues rather than an exact copied sentence.
techniques.why_it_matters: The same passage can produce several valid statements, but only one may answer the exact prompt.
techniques.common_error: Selecting a true detail when the prompt asks for the writer’s overall purpose.

techniques.name: Gist Compression
techniques.purpose: To reduce a passage to its central message before looking closely at distractors.
how_to: Identify the repeated topic or concept.
Read the opening and concluding sentences carefully.
Notice which idea receives the most explanation or support.
State the passage in one short sentence without minor examples.
techniques.example: A passage describes several ways technology reaches remote learners. A useful gist is: “Technology expands access to education in isolated areas.”
techniques.why_it_matters: A clear gist protects you from options that repeat memorable details but miss the central point.
techniques.common_error: Treating the most surprising example as the main idea.

techniques.name: Evidence Ladder for Inference
techniques.purpose: To draw conclusions without guessing beyond the text.
how_to: Find two or more relevant clues.
Ask what conclusion naturally connects those clues.
Reject conclusions that require new facts not supplied by the writer.
Choose the weakest claim that is still fully supported rather than the strongest imaginable claim.
techniques.example: If a passage says a service is available in every region and across every category, a safe inference is that it is widespread, not that every person uses it.
techniques.why_it_matters: Inference questions reward logical reading, not imagination or outside knowledge.

techniques.name: Writer-Attitude Detection
techniques.purpose: To identify approval, criticism, uncertainty, surprise, or neutrality through word choice.
how_to: Underline evaluative adjectives, adverbs, and verbs.
Compare positive and negative alternatives.
Notice quotation marks, contrast markers, and qualifying language.
Decide whether the writer reports information neutrally or comments on it.
techniques.example: “Sun-baked countryside” can create a warmer or more attractive image than “sunburnt countryside,” which may suggest damage or discomfort.
techniques.why_it_matters: Two descriptions can refer to the same place while expressing very different attitudes.
techniques.common_error: Ignoring connotation because the literal topic remains the same.

techniques.name: Option Paraphrasing
techniques.purpose: To expose the real meaning of complicated answer choices.
how_to: Replace formal vocabulary with simpler words.
Identify the subject, action, cause, and result in the option.
Mark qualifiers such as “mainly,” “some,” “only,” or “generally.”
Compare the simplified meaning with the passage rather than matching isolated words.
techniques.example: “The initiative facilitated educational provision in isolated communities” becomes “The program helped provide education in remote places.”
techniques.why_it_matters: Correct answers commonly paraphrase the passage rather than copy it.
techniques.common_error: Rejecting the correct answer because it uses different vocabulary from the text.

techniques.name: Distractor Diagnosis
techniques.purpose: To eliminate options for clear, repeatable reasons.
how_to: Mark an option C if it contradicts the passage.
Mark it NM if it is not mentioned or supported.
Mark it PT if it is only partly true.
Mark it SD if it focuses on a supporting detail instead of the main point.
Mark it EX if it exaggerates the passage.
Keep only options that match both the evidence and the prompt.
techniques.example: A passage says online learning can improve access. An option claiming it has completely replaced classroom teaching is an exaggeration.
techniques.why_it_matters: Naming the reason for rejection prevents emotional or vocabulary-based guessing.
techniques.common_error: Keeping an option because one phrase appears in the passage even though the complete statement is wrong.

techniques.name: Context-Clue Vocabulary
techniques.purpose: To infer unfamiliar words without stopping to translate everything.
how_to: Read the full sentence containing the word.
Check the sentence before and after it.
Look for definitions, examples, contrasts, causes, results, and synonyms.
Break the word into prefixes, roots, and suffixes.
Substitute a possible meaning and test whether the sentence remains logical.
techniques.example: In “special provision was made for inaccessible outback communities,” the references to remote regions and special delivery methods suggest that “inaccessible” means difficult to reach.
techniques.why_it_matters: The passage usually supplies enough clues to understand the function of a word even when its exact dictionary definition is unknown.
techniques.common_error: Spending excessive time defining a word that is irrelevant to the question.

techniques.name: Specific-Meaning Shortcut
how_to: Read the target word or phrase in the prompt.
Locate it or its possible matches in the passage.
Read the surrounding clause and sentence.
Test each option as a replacement in that context.
Select the option that preserves the sentence’s intended meaning.
techniques.example: When asked which passage word means “residences,” inspect words such as “homes,” “buildings,” and “settlements” in their sentences rather than choosing by dictionary similarity alone.
techniques.why_it_matters: A word may have several meanings, but only one fits its use in the passage.
techniques.common_error: Reading the entire passage for gist before answering a narrowly focused vocabulary question.

worked_examples.title: Inferring Tone from Word Choice
worked_examples.input: Sentence A: “Travellers crossed the sun-baked region.” Sentence B: “Travellers crossed the sunburnt region.” Prompt: Which expression presents the region more positively?
worked_examples.decoding: The prompt asks about writer attitude and connotation, not the physical temperature of the region.
worked_examples.plan: Compare the emotional associations of “sun-baked” and “sunburnt.” Decide which phrase sounds more attractive or neutral and which suggests harm.
worked_examples.model_answer: “Sun-baked region” is the more positive description because “baked” can suggest warmth and a dry landscape, whereas “sunburnt” suggests damage caused by excessive heat.

annotations.comment: Writer attitude and connotation.
Both phrases describe heat, but they create different emotional impressions.
“Sunburnt” normally carries an association of pain or damage.
Choose according to contextual tone, not literal topic similarity.

worked_examples.title: Working Out an Unfamiliar Word
worked_examples.input: Passage: “Special arrangements were introduced for inaccessible inland communities, with digital classrooms bringing lessons to students in the most isolated districts.” Prompt: What does “inaccessible” most nearly mean in this passage? A. Unpopular B. Difficult to reach C. Poorly educated D. Recently established
worked_examples.decoding: This is a vocabulary-in-context question. The phrase “in this passage” requires the meaning that fits the surrounding sentence.
worked_examples.plan: Use “special arrangements,” “inland communities,” “digital classrooms,” and “isolated districts” as clues. Substitute each option into the sentence.

annotations.comment: “Isolated districts” suggests geographical remoteness.
Digital classrooms are used because ordinary physical access is difficult.
The passage gives no information about popularity.
Education level and age of settlement are not discussed.

worked_examples.title: Drawing a Supported Inference
worked_examples.input: Passage: “Reports of the offence were recorded in urban centres, farming districts, coastal communities, and remote inland towns. Every category examined showed an increase.” Prompt: Which statement can be inferred? A. The offence occurred only in cities. B. The problem was geographically widespread. C. Rural areas experienced no change. D. Every citizen was affected.
worked_examples.decoding: The prompt asks for an inference. The correct answer may not repeat one exact sentence but must follow logically from the combined evidence.
worked_examples.plan: Identify the range of locations, combine it with the statement that every examined category increased, and reject absolute claims.
worked_examples.model_answer: B. The problem was geographically widespread.

annotations.comment: Urban, farming, coastal, and remote inland locations cover many kinds of areas.
Occurrence across many regions supports “geographically widespread.”
Options A and C conflict directly with the locations listed.
Option D changes widespread occurrence into an unsupported claim about every citizen.

worked_examples.title: Matching a Word to Its Passage Meaning
worked_examples.input: Passage: “The university converted several former offices into student dwellings. These residences are located close to the main library, while temporary shelters are available during emergencies.” Prompt: Which word in the passage has the closest meaning to “residences”? A. Offices B. Dwellings C. Library D. Shelters
worked_examples.decoding: The task asks for a contextual synonym. Several options are places or buildings, but only one has the same meaning in this sentence.
worked_examples.plan: Locate every possible place word, check its role in context, and determine which one directly refers to places where students live.

annotations.comment: “Student dwellings” means places where students live.
The offices were converted; they were not originally residences in this context.
A library is a study facility, not accommodation.
Shelters may provide temporary accommodation, but the sentence distinguishes them from the residences.

worked_examples.title: Identifying the Writer’s Main Purpose
worked_examples.input: Passage: “Many institutions have introduced online lectures because they offer flexibility. However, students still value direct discussion with lecturers and classmates. For this reason, several universities now combine digital materials with face-to-face seminars.” Prompt: The writer’s main purpose is to: A. argue that classroom teaching should end; B. explain why universities use a blended approach; C. criticize students who dislike technology; D. prove that online learning is cheaper.
worked_examples.decoding: The prompt asks for the writer’s purpose across the whole passage.
worked_examples.plan: Summarize the structure: benefit of online learning, continuing value of direct interaction, and resulting combined approach.
worked_examples.model_answer: B. Explain why universities use a blended approach.

annotations.comment: The passage moves from one benefit to a limitation and then to a combined solution.
The writer explains the reason for blending online and face-to-face learning.
The passage supports continued face-to-face seminars.
Student criticism and cost are not discussed.

items.item: The passage is mainly concerned with...
items.when_to_use: Recognize this as a gist or main-idea prompt.

items.item: The writer mentions X in order to...
items.when_to_use: Recognize this as a writer’s-purpose or paragraph-function prompt.
Look for a conclusion strongly supported by clues rather than an exact sentence.
Select information directly stated or clearly paraphrased in the text.

items.item: In the passage, the word X most nearly means...
items.when_to_use: Use local context and test possible replacements.
Expect a contrast, qualification, or change in direction.
Identify a conclusion, effect, or outcome.

items.item: for example / for instance / such as
items.when_to_use: Separate supporting examples from the main claim.
Compare opposing groups, ideas, trends, or viewpoints.
Look for a restatement or explanation that may clarify difficult vocabulary.
Recognize strong certainty or confidence.
Recognize limited certainty or an appearance that may not be fully confirmed.
Recognize negative evaluation or disappointment.
Recognize the writer’s sense that information is unexpected.
Avoid answer options that turn possibility into certainty.
Reject an answer that states the opposite of the passage.

items.item: This option is not supported because...
items.when_to_use: Reject an answer that introduces an idea absent from the text.

items.item: This option is only partly true...
items.when_to_use: Reject an answer whose first part matches but whose complete claim is inaccurate.

items.item: This option focuses on a minor detail...
items.when_to_use: Reject a supporting example when the prompt asks for gist or purpose.

items.item: This option is too strong because...
items.when_to_use: Reject an exaggerated answer containing absolute or universal language.
Use the following phrase as a direct definition.
Infer meaning through contrast.
Infer a category from listed examples.
Use the stated reason to infer the meaning or function of an unfamiliar expression.
Use the result to understand the cause or preceding concept.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the options before understanding the prompt.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The options can influence your interpretation and make you search for the wrong kind of information.
common_mistakes.fix: Classify the prompt first and decide what evidence a correct answer must contain.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing an option because it repeats words from the passage.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Distractors often copy vocabulary while changing the relationship, cause, attitude, or conclusion.
common_mistakes.fix: Compare complete meanings and paraphrase the option before selecting it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading every passage in exactly the same way.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A vocabulary question may require only local context, while a gist or inference question requires broader reading.
common_mistakes.fix: Match the reading route to the prompt type.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using outside knowledge to improve or correct the passage.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: An option can be factually reasonable but still unsupported by the given text.
common_mistakes.fix: Require textual evidence for every selection.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating an inference as a guess.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Unsupported conclusions go beyond what the writer allows.
common_mistakes.fix: Build the inference from at least one strong clue, preferably two connected clues.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Changing a qualified claim into an absolute claim alters its meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Underline qualifiers in both the passage and options.

common_mistakes.mistake: Selecting a minor supporting point as the main idea.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A memorable example may be accurate but too narrow to represent the whole passage.
common_mistakes.fix: Ask which option covers the largest proportion of the passage without becoming vague.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping to define every unfamiliar word.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Some words are irrelevant to the question and can consume valuable time.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the prompt and options first, then investigate only words that affect the decision.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a fixed number of answers in multiple-answer items.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: This encourages over-selection or under-selection without evidence.
common_mistakes.fix: Judge each option independently as supported or unsupported.

common_mistakes.mistake: Failing to re-read the prompt before submitting.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A learner may find a true statement but answer the wrong question.
common_mistakes.fix: Perform a final prompt-to-answer alignment check.

time_budget.focus: Review gist, detail, purpose, organization, inference, explicit information, implicit information, and categorization.
Classify prompts and choose the correct reading route before reading any passage.
Compress short academic passages into one-sentence summaries and identify paragraph functions.
Combine textual clues and analyze evaluative vocabulary, tone, and degree of certainty.
Use definitions, examples, contrast, word parts, cause, and result to infer meanings.
Paraphrase choices and label distractors as contradiction, not mentioned, partial truth, minor detail, or exaggeration.
Complete both single-answer and multiple-answer items without pausing for full dictionary-style analysis.
Record the reason for every incorrect answer and select one strategy to improve.

drills.name: Prompt Sorting
drills.instructions: Collect ten prompts and label each one GIST, PURPOSE, DETAIL, INFERENCE, ORGANIZATION, CATEGORY, or VOCABULARY. State the best reading route for each.

drills.name: Ten-Word Gist
drills.instructions: Read a short passage and summarize its central message in no more than ten words. Then compare your summary with each answer option.

drills.name: Evidence Underlining
drills.instructions: For every selected answer, underline the exact sentence or connected clues that support it. Do not accept an answer without visible evidence.

drills.name: Option Translation
drills.instructions: Rewrite each option in simple English while preserving qualifiers, causes, and comparisons. Reject options only after paraphrasing them.

drills.name: Distractor Labelling
drills.instructions: Label wrong options C for contradiction, NM for not mentioned, PT for partly true, SD for supporting detail, and EX for exaggeration.

drills.name: Inference Ladder
drills.instructions: Write clue one, clue two, and the safest supported conclusion. Check that the conclusion does not introduce new information.

drills.name: Context Replacement
drills.instructions: Replace an unfamiliar word with each answer option and read the sentence again. Select the replacement that preserves meaning and grammar.

drills.name: Single-versus-Multiple Control
drills.instructions: Complete paired items based on the same passage: one single-answer question and one multiple-answer question. Explain how the selection rule changes.

practice_plan.routine: Use a three-pass routine: first decode the prompt and make a quick passage map; second evaluate and paraphrase every serious option using evidence; third re-read the prompt, remove unsupported selections, and record the reason for any uncertainty in an error log.

mastery_checklist: I can identify the reading skill required by the prompt before reading the options in detail.
I can explain the difference between a gist question and a detailed-information question.
I can identify the writer’s purpose for including an example, contrast, definition, or statistic.
I can distinguish directly stated information from a reasonable inference.
I can combine clues to form a conclusion without adding outside assumptions.
I can recognize positive, negative, neutral, and uncertain attitudes through word choice.
I can paraphrase complicated options without losing important qualifiers.
I can identify distractors that are contradicted, unsupported, partly true, too narrow, or exaggerated.
I can infer an unfamiliar word through context and word structure.
I can recognize when a vocabulary prompt requires local reading instead of a full gist analysis.
I can judge each option independently in a multiple-answer item.
I can support every selected answer with a specific sentence or logical evidence chain.
I can complete practice items within a controlled time without defining every unfamiliar word.
I can explain why each rejected option is wrong, not merely why my chosen answer seems right.
strategy_notes: The prompt controls the strategy. Do not use one fixed reading method for every item.
For broad inference questions, reading the passage before studying the options reduces confusion and confirmation bias.
For specific word-meaning questions, begin with the target sentence and nearby context rather than summarizing the entire passage.
A correct inference is not directly copied, but it is still securely tied to textual evidence.
The safest inference is usually moderate. Be suspicious when an option is more certain or more universal than the passage.
Main-idea answers should cover the passage broadly while remaining specific enough to reflect the writer’s real focus.
Writer-purpose questions often depend on paragraph function: introduce, explain, compare, challenge, illustrate, or conclude.
A familiar word may have an unfamiliar contextual meaning, so test possible meanings inside the original sentence.
When two options appear possible, compare their qualifiers and scope rather than choosing the one with more matching vocabulary.
In multiple-answer tasks, do not select an option that is only half correct; the complete statement must be supported.
Efficient readers ignore difficult words that do not affect the prompt or answer choices.
Keep an error log organized by mistake type, such as prompt confusion, vocabulary, inference, over-selection, or distractor attraction.

metadata.estimated_study_time: Plan about 2 hours for this lesson, with time for reading-skill review, prompt analysis, unfamiliar-word strategies, practice items, and self-checking.
